title: Dynamic limiter and anomaly-driven routing for safe config rollouts
creator: Ravi Patel
description:
Goal: Enable automated batching/caching recommendation application with strong latency and throughput guardrails. We will implement a dynamic limiter service + SLO-aware routing layer and an anomaly detector that can trigger automated rollback or narrow the rollout window when risk is detected. This ticket covers design, prototype, and integration with the rollout controller used by OptimizeKit.

Background:
- Current cost-optimizer suggests batching/caching profile changes but applying them at scale can cause p95 latency regressions under certain tail-heavy traffic shapes. Existing work (ENG-7831, ENG-9142) introduced SLO-aware suggestions and advisor flows but lacks automated runtime guardrails for safe config apply/rollback.

Success criteria:
- Automated rollouts of batching/caching configs limited by dynamic token/sec and in-flight request caps based on historical load shape and target SLOs.
- SLO-aware routing that routes a % of traffic to the new config based on SLO headroom and latency distributions, not just static percentages.
- Anomaly detector that monitors key signals (p50/p95/p99 latency, error-rate, queue depth, GPU utilization, token throughput) and triggers immediate rollback or step-down of rollout when thresholds are crossed.
- Integration tests and chaos tests showing rollback within TTL (<= 60s) for severe regressions; system can safely converge to recommended config under normal conditions and realize >= 10% token-cost reduction on typical demo workloads without SLO breaches.

Design decisions and trade-offs:
1) Dynamic limiter vs static caps: dynamic limiter calculates allowed request concurrency and tokens/sec per rollout based on a moving percentile of baseline traffic. Trade-off: increased complexity and risk of tuner bugs vs much better utilization. We will implement a conservative default (clamp to 0.5x observed short-term baseline) and allow experiments to open the clamp.
2) SLO-aware routing mechanics: two options considered: (A) routing based on headroom fraction (recommended) — compute headroom = (SLO - p95_current) / (SLO - p50) and map to traffic weights; (B) Bayesian safe-occupancy model that estimates probability of SLO breach. Option A chosen for initial rollout for simplicity and interpretability.
3) Anomaly detection: start with rule-based detector (threshold + brief rate-of-change checks) to ensure predictable failure modes and fast triggers. Plan to iterate to an ML-based detector once we have labeled incidents.
4) Rollback policies: immediate hard rollback on severe signals (p95 increase > 30% or error rate > 0.5%) and staged roll-down for mild anomalies.

Implementation plan (high level):
- Phase 1 (spike/prototype): implement dynamic limiter library and a minimal SLO-routing controller, add rule-based anomaly detector. (Owner: Sofia)
- Phase 2 (integration): wire into rollout controller used by OptimizeKit, add metrics and dashboards, end-to-end tests and canary job in CI. (Owner: Sofia + SRE)
- Phase 3 (experiment): run experiments against a set of internal workloads, iterate thresholds, and add automatic rollback flows. (Owner: Product + SRE)

Telemetry and dashboards:
- New dashboard panels: rollout weight, limiter allowance, headroom metric, anomaly event rate, time-to-rollback.
- Alerting: SLO-breach alerting will be tuned to avoid noisy signals by correlating anomaly detector events with rollout ids.

Open questions:
- Best default mapping from headroom -> weight. Current plan: conservative sigmoid mapping that gives 0-10% weight for <10% headroom, 10-50% for moderate, up to 100% only when headroom > 50%.
- How to represent multi-model deployments where different model sizes have different cost/latency trade-offs. Proposed short-term: per-model config with shared limiter; long-term: per-model adaptive limiters.

Artifacts and references:
- Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/OPT/Dynamic+Limiter+Design
- Prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/optimizekit/pull/462
- Canary dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/opt/optimize-rollouts
- Incident notes (ENG-2025-09 slow tail incident): https://redwood.ai/incident/2025-09-tail-latency

Next steps:
- Complete prototype PR review and bench test on dedicated staging GPUs (ETA: 2026-03-05).
- Run chaos tests with synthetic tail traffic and validate rollback TTL <= 60s (ETA: 2026-03-18).
- Coordinate with PM for experiment cohorts and opt-in list for initial rollout.
comments: 2026-02-10 - Ravi Patel: Spike complete. Implemented dynamic limiter PoC that calculates allowance from 95th-percentile baseline. Observed deterministic allowance under steady load. Added unit tests for limiter math.
2026-02-17 - Sofia Chen: Design review with PM/SRE. Agreed to start with rule-based anomaly detection and headroom->weight mapping. Action: prepare PR for limiter library and small controller loop.

2026-02-26 - Sofia Chen: Opened prototype PR (https://github.com/redwood-inference/optimizekit/pull/462). Initial CI failing on flakiness in limiter when traffic sim has bursts; adding smoother exponential moving average window.

2026-03-01 - Arun Iyer (SRE): Load tests against staging show p95 sensitivity to aggressive batching when concurrency > 2x baseline. Proposed adding hard concurrency clamp and GPU queue depth monitor to anomaly rules.
2026-03-04 - Sofia Chen: Added GPU queue depth metric and tightened hard rollback thresholds. Updated design doc to include rollback TTL and post-rollback analysis checklist.

2026-03-08 - QA: Synthetic tail test produced a triggered rollback in 42s for a p95 spike of 42% (pass). Noted a false-positive during cold-start bursts; adding a short grace window for new deployments.
2026-03-10 - Ravi Patel: Merging limiter improvements after addressing EMA smoothing and grace window. Next: coordinate with product to select three internal services for beta experiments.
